analysis.one_liner: Makes the low 15% tax rate on stock dividends permanent instead of letting it expire.
analysis.headline: A bill to make the low 15% dividend tax rate permanent was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and died without a hearing, a vote, or any action before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The tax cuts passed in 2003 lowered the tax rate on stock dividends and were set to expire at the end of 2010. This bill would have removed that expiration date, making the low dividend rate permanent. It was introduced late in the 111th Congress by a Republican member with 16 cosponsors and never received a hearing or vote in the Ways and Means Committee, so it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who receive dividend income — overwhelmingly households at the top of the income scale, since most dividend income goes to high earners — would keep paying the 15% rate rather than seeing it rise toward ordinary income tax rates. Corporations would also benefit from a more favorable climate for paying dividends.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy stock investors with dividend income

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 2010 expiration date in the 2003 tax law, keeping the reduced individual tax rate on dividends in place permanently instead of letting it lapse to ordinary income rates.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — and by extension taxpayers generally — forgoes the revenue that would come from taxing dividends at higher rates; without an offset, the permanent rate cut adds to deficits or pressures future spending cuts.

drawbacks.text: The tax cuts it would make permanent flow overwhelmingly to high-income households, so the bill protects the lowest-taxed rate on investment income for those least in need of it.
Permanently cutting the dividend tax rate reduces federal revenue indefinitely, adding to deficits or forcing other taxes or spending cuts to make up the difference.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was designed to prevent a scheduled tax increase on dividend income. The benefit accrues overwhelmingly to wealthy households that own most dividend-paying stock; the cost is roughly $100 billion or more per year in forgone revenue that would otherwise come from those households, adding to deficits or requiring cuts or taxes elsewhere. Even its supporters would acknowledge the dividend rate cut primarily benefits top earners, while the honest counterargument is that higher rates could discourage investment in dividend-paying companies. As introduced, the bill was narrow (dividends only, not capital gains rates it referenced in the CRS title) and received no committee action or debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Representative Scott Garrett of New Jersey introduced the bill on September 29, 2010, with 16 Republican cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the same day; no further action was ever recorded.
The bill would have repealed the sunset in the 2003 Jobs and Growth Tax Relief Reconciliation Act, making the reduced individual tax rate on dividend income permanent.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and all legislation not enacted died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No outcome changed for taxpayers — the dividend rate cuts were allowed to reach their scheduled sunset as written, and no House Democrat ever had to take a position. Wealthy dividend recipients neither gained nor lost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; bill died in committee

for.name: Rep. Scott Garrett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the reduced dividend tax rate permanent.

for.name: 16 of 178 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all Republicans, including Representatives Pence, Hensarling, and Gohmert.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 16 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported it, and the Democratic-controlled House never took it up.

industries.note: A permanent 15% rate rather than a return to ordinary income rates directly increases after-tax returns on dividend income, which goes mainly to high-income households.
A permanent lower dividend rate lowers the tax disadvantage of paying dividends versus buybacks, slightly shaping how companies return profits to shareholders.
